[MUQATIL:53:3-9/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The highest horizon is the direction of the sunrise.

[ZAJJAJ:v5p70/r7] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | rejects | Zajjāj rejects the joint-subject reading as poor outside poetry: استويت أنا وزيد is acceptable, while استويت وزيد is considered ugly.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p70/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | He prefers that Gabriel alone stood at the highest horizon in his true form: Gabriel normally appeared to the Prophet as a man, and at the Prophet's wish he appeared in the east and filled the horizon.
[IBNABIHATIM:v10p3318#4/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud reports that the Prophet saw Gabriel in his true form only twice: once when he asked and Gabriel filled the horizon, and once while ascending with him; this verse refers to the latter occasion.
[NAHHAS:v4p265/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | prefers | Abū Jaʿfar prefers parsing the verb as a circumstantial clause meaning Gabriel rose high.
[NAHHAS:v4p265/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ says both Muḥammad and Gabriel rose, making the pronoun refer to Gabriel and coordinating it with an implicit subject.
[NAHHAS:v4p265/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | Abū Jaʿfar rejects the coordination because an unmarked hidden nominative pronoun cannot be conjoined without emphasis or extended wording.
[NAHHAS:v4p265/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | He also rejects al-Farrāʾ’s Qurʾanic analogy because its context is extended and its pronoun explicit. | mentions 13:5
[NAHHAS:v4p265/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | rejects | The explicit plural pronoun in قمنا وزيد is easier to coordinate than a singular implicit pronoun.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p229/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير وعاصم وابن عامر | reports | Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir open the endings throughout the sūra; Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim also opens them all.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p229/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة والكسائي | reports | Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī use imāla throughout the sūra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p229/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو ونافع | reports | Abū ʿAmr and Nāfiʿ use a pronunciation between fatḥ and kasr.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p229/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | Al-Qaṭʿī’s transmission from ʿUbayd reports imāla for الأفق الأعلى and ثم دنا فتدلى, while ولعلا بعضهم is read open. | mentions 53:8, 23:91
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p229/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī accepts both leaving alif uninclined and using imāla; the mild inclination of Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr is good.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p391/r16] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · السدي | reports | The one at the highest horizon is Gabriel, seen there by Muhammad.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p391/r17] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عكرمة | reports | Alternatively, Muhammad is the one who saw Gabriel at the highest horizon.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p391/r18] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | The highest horizon is the place where the sun rises.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p391/r19] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · قتادة | reports | It is the horizon from which daylight comes, meaning daybreak.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p391/r20] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن زيد | reports | It is the sky's horizon, one of its sides.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p247/r17] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The one at the highest horizon is Gabriel.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p14/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | Al-Wahidi rejects al-Farra's grammatical argument: “he” refers to Gabriel, and the wāw is circumstantial, not coordination; the verb istawā takes one subject, as in 28:14 and 20:5. | mentions 28:14, 20:5
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p14/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | rejects | The phrase is a nominative predicate containing a pronoun for the subject, not an adverb attached to istawā; it therefore does not prove that an overt nominative may coordinate with an unreinforced nominative pronoun. | mentions 28:14, 20:5
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p14/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · عطاء عن ابن عباس | reports | Ata reports Ibn Abbas that the Prophet saw Gabriel in his true form at the highest horizon, with six hundred wings; al-Kalbi gives a similar report.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p14/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل والكلبي | reports | Muqatil places the horizon toward the sunrise; al-Kalbi calls it the sunrise, which the exegetes generally identify as above the east.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p14/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · المفسرون | reports | The exegetes say Gabriel usually came in human form; at Muhammad's request he appeared twice in his angelic form, once at Hira filling the eastern-to-western horizon, where Muhammad fainted, and once in heaven at the Lote Tree. | mentions 81:23, 53:8
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:53:1-8/r8] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The Prophet asked to see Gabriel in his original form and arranged a meeting at Hira; Gabriel appeared from the east and filled the horizon from east to west.
[JISHUMI:v9p6633/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Istiwaʾ originally means balance and can denote dominance, intention, or settling; al-ufuq is a side of the sky, plural āfāq.
[JISHUMI:v9p6633/r14] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A poetic line uses āfāq for the horizons.
[JISHUMI:v9p6635/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Two parses for huwa are given: an independent subject and predicate, or coordination with the fāʾ in fastawā.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The pronoun refers to Muhammad; Arabic usually makes the coordinated pronoun explicit, as in “he and so-and-so,” and rarely omits it. The verse 27:67 provides a parallel. | mentions 27:67
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | One interpretation is that Gabriel and Muhammad appeared at the highest horizon on the Night Journey.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | reports | Alternatively, “he appeared” refers to Gabriel standing in his created form at the highest horizon.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Gabriel normally came in human form; Muhammad asked to see his original form and saw it twice, on earth and in heaven.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r5] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | On earth, Gabriel appeared from the east while Muhammad was at Ḥirāʾ, spanning the horizon; Muhammad fainted, as in 53:8. | mentions 53:8
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v7p400#2/r6] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The second sighting was at the Lote Tree of the Furthest Boundary; no other prophet saw Gabriel in that form.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r10] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الربيع والزجاج | reports | Those who identify the one mighty in power as Gabriel take istawā of him: at Ḥirāʾ he filled the upper horizon with six hundred wings, then drew near Muḥammad; this was also his majestic second descent at the Lote Tree.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r11] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الطبري والفراء | reports | Al-Ṭabarī and al-Farrāʾ likewise take istawā to mean that Gabriel rose.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | Here huwa refers to Muḥammad, mentioned in the pronoun of ʿallamahu; grammarians dislike coordinating an unreinforced nominative pronoun, though al-Farrāʾ cites poetry for it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ cites a poetic example of coordinating an unreinforced nominative pronoun.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | reports | The referents could instead be reversed, with Muḥammad as the subject of istawā and Gabriel as huwa.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r15] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes al-aʿlā to mean the crown of the head and what accompanies it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r16] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda identify the upper horizon specifically as the place where the sun rises; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this restriction has no evidence.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r7] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الحسن | reports | In al-Ḥasan's reading, istawā has God as its subject, the one described as mighty in power.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAṭiyya accordingly takes the upper horizon as an attribute of God's greatness, power, and dominion, comparable to His istiwā over the Throne. | mentions 20:5
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p196#2/r9] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The divine reading of istawā is linked to the statement that the Merciful istawā over the Throne. | mentions 20:5
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p197/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | prefers | Ibn Atiyya's correct view is that all these descriptions concern Gabriel: 53:13 says Muhammad saw him on another descent, implying an earlier one, and no report says Muhammad saw God before the Night Journe

[QURTUBI-FULL:53:5-7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ notes that Arabic usually makes the pronoun explicit when coordinating a subject pronoun, though omission occurs; his line about the nabʿ and kharūʿ supplies poetic evidence.

[QURTUBI-FULL:53:6-10/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | prefers | The correct reading is Gabriel in his original form: Muḥammad had seen him as a man and wanted to see his true form, so Gabriel filled the eastern horizon.

[QURTUBI-FULL:53:6-10/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Ufuq means a side or region of the sky and its plural is āfāq; the word also varies as ufuq/ufuq.

[BAYDAWI-FULL:53:5-8/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The pronoun refers to Gabriel, who was at the upper horizon of the sky.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p188#3/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | “He” is Gabriel, located at the highest horizon, glossed as the sunrise point.

[SAMIN-DURR:53:7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · مكي | reports | On the first parse, the clause may be circumstantial from the subject of استوى; Makkī states this option.
[SAMIN-DURR:53:7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, the clause is a resumption in which God reports this fact.

[SAMIN-DURR:53:7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Other reports assign استوى to Gabriel and هو to Muhammad, or reverse the referents.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p444#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The one standing at the highest horizon is Gabriel.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p444#2/r10] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | rejects | The first vision of Gabriel in this form happened before the Night Journey, while the second was at the Lote Tree during the Journey, so the two could not have jointly stood at the horizon that night.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v7p454/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن مسعود (على ظن محمد) | reports | A report tentatively attributed to Ibn Masud says Muhammad saw Gabriel in his form twice: once when requested, when Gabriel filled the horizon, and again on the ascent. [BIQAI-FULL:v7p313#2/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The scene is when the Prophet saw Gabriel seated on a chair between heaven and earth, filling the horizon.
[BIQAI-FULL:v7p313#2/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The main reading identifies the pronoun with Gabriel at the highest region of heaven; another possible reading identifies the Prophet, with Gabriel standing with him.

[BURSEVI:v9p178/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The horizon is the boundary between visible and unseen portions of the celestial sphere; the upper horizon is sunrise, unlike the lower western horizon, so Gabriel is at the eastern edge of the world.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Prophet's night ascent represents total annihilation: night manifests fanāʾ, and its seven stages correspond to seven divine names, ending with al-Qayyūm and al-Qahhār.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Night symbolizes annihilation and day subsistence; the seven annihilation stations correspond to seven names, while Mecca's seven sanctuary minarets signify them.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The Prophet's sanctuary has five minarets for the five subsistence stations signified by the five remaining names, ending in al-Ahad al-Samad.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | He calculates seven names at one hundred each, giving seven hundred; Gabriel's lower annihilation station stops at the Lote Tree, while the Prophet proceeds to the Throne and overcomes it.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Gabriel's journey ends at the name al-Qayyūm, where the Prophet's course subdues him; Gabriel remains to convey revelation that gives hearts life, hence his title Spirit of Holiness.
[BURSEVI:v9p178/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Gabriel has six hundred of the seven hundred wings in image and meaning, while the Prophet has seven hundred spiritual wings; prophetic power therefore exceeds ange

[ALUSI-FULL:v27p48/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The prepositional phrase attaches to استوى; coordinating a subject pronoun without a separator is allowed by Kufans, though most reject that sense here.
[ELMALILI:53:1-7#2/r19] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | Elmalili prefers the Prophet as the subject: after Gabriel taught him, Muhammad rose and attained steadiness in knowledge and prophethood at the highest horizon.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p95/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The fa in he stood elaborates on Gabriel's teaching by the angel of strong powers.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p95/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The pronoun certainly refers to Gabriel and situates his readiness before he descended to the earthly world.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p95/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | An horizon is the visible sky-space where the earth's far limit appears to meet the blue dome; it commonly means a distant direction, as in east and west horizons.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p95/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The qualifier highest shows this is a region of the heavenly sky and sets up the next statement that Gabriel approached.
